newsitem.title: PERU: Peru's Fujimori plans to wipe out rebels in region.
newsitem.headline: Peru's Fujimori plans to wipe out rebels in region.

text.p: Peruvian President Alberto Fujimori vowed on Thursday to wipe out the Marxist group holding 73 hostages at the Japanese ambassador's residence in Lima once the crisis was over.

"This is not going to go unpunished," Fujimori said in La Paz, Bolivia. "We are looking for the total erradication of the group in the region," he said, referring to the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA).

Speaking with reporters during a brief visit with Bolivian President Gonzalo Sanchez de Lozada, Fujimori said he would not let up in his fight against terrorism that he claimed had virtually defeated rebel groups in Peru.
"There is no going back. There are still isolated groups ... this government is going to hunt them down," he said.
Fujimori's threatening tone underlined police tactics over the last few days that have steadily tightened the screws on the defiant MRTA rebels.

Shortly before dawn on Thursday, four carpenters arrived to board up one of the compound's two entrances and a small hole in the wall used by service staff. Watched by a group of policemen, the labourers spent about an hour nailing wooden planks across the two access points.
Their action left open only the entrance that has been used by Red Cross workers, mediators and freed captives.
A police helicopter also flew over the mined and booby-trapped residence several times.

The MRTA responded to the government's latest move on the Internet, slamming Fujimori as a "dictator" and calling on international opinion to help prevent a "massacre" by the government at the residence.
"We have to stop the dictator now. We do not have to suffer five years more," said a new MRTA communique.

A second communique added that the police activities were "provocations that seek a pretext to justify military intervention ... We ask for the families, the press, human rights organisations and national and international solidarity to help prevent this massacre we warn of."
Continuing the propaganda war from within the residence, the rebels chanted together, unfurled a new banner and shouted slogans to reporters outside.

"We will carry on until we die. We will not back down in our efforts," they shouted, local Radio Programas del Peru said. "The families of our prisoners are also waiting for them in their homes. Peace for all Peruvians," read the banner's message, in blue letters on a white bed sheet.

In their war of nerves with the MRTA, the police have driven armoured personnel carriers with heavy machine guns within a few blocks of the residence. Their special force officers have approached the compound's walls, tossed stones into the driveway, peeked around the gate and run backward and forward in a seeming effort to unnerve the MRTA.
Before leaving for Bolivia, Fujimori publicly reiterated the government's refusal to consider the rebels main demand for the release of about 400 jailed comrades.
"We are not going to allow (government negotiator Domingo) Palermo to go to the negotiating table unless they accept that there will be no release of prisoners," Fujimori said.

The government's firm line on the MRTA prisoners has become the sticking point in moves to negotiate a solution to the crisis. Both sides say they are willing in principle to talk but the rebels insist they will not sit down until their principal demand is included on the agenda.
The MRTA rebels originally seized hundreds of guests when they stormed a cocktail party at the residence on Dec. 17.

They freed most in what they called "goodwill gestures," keeping those they consider the most important bargaining chips, including two Peruvian Cabinet ministers, generals, security chiefs, about two dozen Japanese businessmen and diplomats and ambassadors from Bolivia and Japan.

Congress passed a special law on Thursday allowing captive Foreign Minister Francisco Tudela and Agriculture Minister Rodolfo Munante to stay in their posts despite their prolonged absence from duties.
The MRTA is holding the Bolivian diplomat in the hope of obtaining the release of four rebels jailed in the neighbouring country. Bolivia has from the outset backed Fujimori's stance on prisoners.
